items.summary: A real-life flooding becomes a flashpoint in this novel exploring family relationships, female liberation and the drive for Welsh independence In the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud. Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence.

Our everyday choices can help prevent fires from starting, and work across our lands, yards and homes can interrupt their spread. The hazard resilience portion of Hawaiʻi’s “green fee” funding is an important start toward supporting that work. Prevention begins with care around things that can accidentally ignite a fire: barbecues, campfires, fireworks, equipment and vehicles. Put campfires and cooking fires out cold, use equipment carefully, and keep vehicles off dry grass when driving, parking or idling. These actions help reduce wildfire risk wherever we live, work or visit. Conservation, ecological restoration and agriculture also reduce wildfire risk. Fire departments, counties and state agencies connect these efforts with planning, emergency access, infrastructure and public land management. Working across property boundaries is what makes these individual efforts more effective. A neighborhood’s vegetation management project is strengthened by coordinated work on adjacent lands. Community plans become more useful when residents, emergency responders and neighboring landowners understand their roles and work together to carry them out. This work takes coordination, technical assistance and resources. A community may have a plan but need equipment and crews to carry it out. Funding and supportive policies help turn these opportunities into work on the ground. Resilience Work Needed Government is beginning to make important investments in wildfire resilience, but public funding alone cannot reduce the risks we face. We all have a responsibility to do our part, whether that means preventing sparks, managing vegetation around our homes or working with neighbors and land managers on larger projects. Green fee funding is beginning to support connected parts of the wildfire resilience work Hawaiʻi needs: community risk reduction and Firewise USA efforts, fire management planning for state parks, early wildfire detection, and coordination across these and other initiatives. The Hawaiʻi Urban Interface, or HUI, Wildfire Grant Program shows what investment in locally developed projects can accomplish. Administered by the Department of Land and Natural Resources Division of Forestry and Wildlife in partnership with the Hawaiʻi Wildfire Management Organization, the program awarded $1.8 million to eight organizations across five islands in 2026, up from $1.5 million in 2025. Projects include hazardous vegetation removal, managed grazing, fuel breaks, landscape restoration, emergency access improvements and community planning. We all have a responsibility to do our part. These projects reflect different needs across Hawaiʻi. Some communities are ready for larger landscape projects; others are focused on defensible space around homes, vegetation along neighborhood boundaries, or developing risk assessments and action plans. Other green fee priorities include a statewide fire management plan for state parks and Pūlama I Ka ʻĀina, a statewide early wildfire detection effort through the Department of Law Enforcement. Across Hawaiʻi, communities are putting time and effort into this work. Some have high-impact, shovel-ready projects that need resources. Green fee investment via programs like the HUI Grant Program can help turn that preparation into completed work, reducing identified risks before the next fire starts. Following through means maintaining what we accomplish. Vegetation grows back, fuel breaks need upkeep, temporary measures need to become sustained land management practices, and community plans need to reflect changing conditions. Sustained funding and supportive policies help preserve completed projects’ benefits and allow communities and land managers to take on new priorities. Public investment brings responsibility to show where funding goes, what gets completed and how work will be maintained. Learning from these projects — including what helps them succeed and what gets in the way — can make future investments more effective. The green fee’s wildfire resilience initiatives build on work already underway and provide an important start toward getting more done. Government investment is an important part of that effort, but lasting progress will depend on all of us doing our part to prevent ignitions, reduce the fuels that carry fire, and maintain that work together, across property boundaries and across our whole system.

items.originalTitle: ‘Smart’ Implants Are Driving Up Health Costs — Even When Patients Don’t Ask for Them
items.author: Darius Tahir
items.title: ‘Smart’ Implants Are Driving Up Health Costs — Even When Patients Don’t Ask for Them
items.summary: Steve Russak, 70, of Santa Rosa Valley, California, woke up from knee replacement surgery last year to a text message. It was from the company that made his new knee. Over the next few days, the company, Zimmer Biomet, texted four times. Russak didn’t understand the inquiries asking him to use an app, he said. Finally, a company representative called and offered help setting up some accessories, Russak told KFF Health News. “I said, ‘What? I don’t know what you’re talking about.’” It turned out Russak did not receive just any old replacement of bone and cartilage. He’d had a “smart knee” put in - an artificial joint called the Persona IQ with a lithium-ion battery, sensors, and transmitter that, should he authorize it, would send data about his gait and range of motion to his clinicians and Zimmer. Russak is suing the doctor, Zimmer, and Canary Medical, a health technology company that helped develop the device. In his lawsuit , Russak claims the knee was an “unauthorized implantation” and that, according to Zimmer’s “patient-facing materials,” he should have been given the option to opt out of data collection or decline the knee altogether, but wasn’t. Russak said he doesn’t want to set up the device to collect and transmit data for several reasons, including his privacy. Now that it’s in his body, though, he said it poses potential disruptions. For example, Russak said he recently couldn’t get an MRI because of compatibility issues. Neither the doctor nor the doctor’s lawyer responded to multiple requests for comment. The case is ongoing, with the next hearing scheduled for December. Russak said he has dropped the fraud and breach of fiduciary duty allegations originally filed against the doctor but is continuing to sue on other grounds, including lack of informed consent. The doctor has yet to respond to the complaint in court. Both Zimmer and Canary filed initial responses denying “each and every allegation” in Russak’s complaint. They have offered a variety of defenses, including that any damages are the fault of another party or, as Zimmer’s response said, caused by actions or reactions “not reasonably foreseeable.” Canary Medical did not respond to requests for comment. Zimmer spokesperson Troy Kirkpatrick declined to comment on lawsuits against the company but said that “nearly 90%” of surveyed patients who received Zimmer’s joint replacements report they would choose an orthopedic device with remote monitoring capabilities again in the future. “The transmission of post-operative recovery data requires patient authorization at the time the patient sets up an account and is designed to support patient-surgeon relationships and postoperative care,” Kirkpatrick said in an emailed statement. He added that Zimmer takes privacy and compliance with regulations “very seriously.” Steve Russak says he didn’t understand the text messages he received after knee replacement surgery asking him to use an app. He later learned he’d had a smart knee put in, he says. (Hannah Norman/KFF Health News) The smart knee is part of a burgeoning trend in American medicine. While Zimmer introduced its device as “ the world’s first and only ” FDA-approved smart knee in 2021, there’s now a range of internet-connected devices - from implants to external products such as blood pressure monitors - that report data about patients’ conditions to doctors or other medical professionals. To proponents, the products offer the chance for better care: They can provide measurements showing whether a patient’s glucose is swerving out of control, for instance. However, enhanced monitoring comes with potential drawbacks, including threats to privacy, and some doctors and researchers caution there is little evidence that smart devices improve health outcomes. There’s “a lot of enthusiasm for remote monitoring technologies. There is tremendous potential,” said Sanket Dhruva, a University of California-San Francisco cardiologist and digital health researcher. But there’s a need for more rigorous data, he said. “We’re getting all this data - is this helping our patients recover better? That’s what we really care about.” Nonetheless, such devices generally mean more money for doctors, who can charge to examine the information they collect. Monitoring Every Step Both Medicare and private insurers reimburse clinical professionals for reviewing data from smart devices. In 2024, nearly 1 million Medicare beneficiaries received that service, known as “remote patient monitoring,” according to the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Inspector General. Medicare, the federal program covering older Americans and some with disabilities, paid medical providers $536 million for remote monitoring, more than double what it paid three years earlier. A review by the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker found about 300,000 adults with employer-sponsored insurance received at least one remote monitoring claim in 2023. Medicare has proposed pulling back on some reimbursements after the department’s inspector general warned remote monitoring poses fraud risks: About 43% of patients in 2024 didn’t receive the full suite of services defined by the program - which includes educating the patient about the device and monitoring data for changes in health. The watchdog also cautioned that companies sometimes cold-call patients to offer and sign them up for devices they may not need. The internet-connected devices may also pose risks to privacy or expose patients to unexpected consequences. In 2018, ProPublica reported that insurers watched the performance of CPAP machines and, determining some patients weren’t using them, denied coverage for replacement supplies such as masks. In the case of Zimmer, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services spokesperson Christopher Krepich emailed KFF Health News that “CMS payment does not mean the agency endorses a manufacturer’s marketing claims or guarantees that a technology improves outcomes for every patient.” He said the agency regularly evaluates its reimbursement policies. Russak’s Medicare account shows the program paid for his surgery and knee implant, but it has not received any claims related to remote monitoring for the device, which he has not set up to transmit data. The smart knee is one of the flagship orthopedic products of Indiana-based Zimmer Biomet, which also manufactures non-connected knee joints. The company - which hired professional strongman, actor, and former California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger to pitch its products as its “chief movement officer” - sold some $3.3 billion in knee joints last year. Russak’s Medicare account shows the program paid for his surgery and knee implant, but it has not received any claims related to remote monitoring for the device, which he has not set up to transmit data. (Hannah Norman/KFF Health News) Up the California coast in Contra Costa County, Jodi Murphy filed a lawsuit against Zimmer, Canary Medical, and her doctor after receiving a Persona IQ knee implant and being registered to use Zimmer’s app. The lawsuit alleges the doctor and companies were at fault because they acted “without disclosing this device or obtaining Plaintiff’s specific informed consent for its use.” The doctor and her practice denied all allegations . Zimmer’s attorneys have said the company “does not practice medicine and as a matter of law had no duty to obtain consent to the treatment provided by her physician.” A hearing is scheduled for February. The doctor did not respond to requests for comment. Murphy and her lawyer declined to comment. Russak’s lawsuit alleges his doctor told him he “had not disclosed the electronic nature, wireless transmission functions, or data-collection capabilities of the Persona IQ to prior patients in whom he had implanted the same device.” It goes on to cite that exchange as evidence that the companies “failed to adequately educate” the doctor. “I don’t believe that Zimmer or Canary are training the doctors, and it’s an issue,” Russak told KFF Health News. Zimmer’s website says the implant allows care teams to “monitor and personalize” a patient’s experience and improve a practice’s efficiency. Many patients prefer the remote option, the company’s literature says. Farther down the webpage, the company says the implant is “not intended to support clinical decision-making” and has “not been shown to provide any clinical benefit.” The company also mentions the potential financial rewards for surgeons who implant the device - including ongoing payments for remote monitoring. ‘Nice-To-Have’ vs. ‘Need-To-Have’ Kevin Bozic, an orthopedic surgeon who is chair of surgery and perioperative care at the University of Texas-Austin, reviewed research on the Zimmer smart knee provided by Zimmer spokesperson Kirkpatrick at KFF Health News’ request. “None of them compare Persona IQ to a more conventional [knee] implant,” he wrote in an email. Bozic said orthopedic surgeons he knows are “ambivalent” about Zimmer’s smart knee devices and many don’t use them. The implant is the “most generic part of the operation and really doesn’t have a big impact at all on the outcome.” In theory, he said, the data collected by the device about the number of steps a patient takes and the joint’s range of motion makes for better care. If a patient becomes more sedentary, that could be a useful signal for clinicians, he said. But, in practice, “it’s a nice-to-have, certainly not a need-to-have,” Bozic said, “certainly not something that I would want to add significant cost to the procedure for.” Surgeons already check on patients and ask to be informed if their health changes, he said. “It’s overkill to have it in the knee.” Smart-knee manufacturers have also profited from a different Medicare benefit - a “new technology add-on payment” - that effectively temporarily subsidizes the adoption of otherwise money-losing new devices, thereby encouraging innovation. (The extra payment for Persona IQ lapsed in fall 2024.) The payment program has undergone several adjustments in recent years. Beginning in late 2020 - until the government adjusted the benefit this year - there was no requirement that new technology substantially improve on older devices or pills. That lack of a requirement, predictably, meant more qualifying therapies. A 2025 study found an average of four approved annually in the near decade before the 2020 change; in the next four fiscal years, the authors said, the average moved up to nearly 15 a year. The subsidy has lasting benefits for the manufacturers, said Dhruva, the UCSF cardiologist, who studies digital technologies and reimbursement. Medicare’s reimbursements are based on the average costs of a procedure. Since the subsidy increases the cost of the procedure, it increases the average costs, too - thereby driving up the basis for future costs. Indeed, Dhruva said, the problem of payments for unproven services is present in Medicare reimbursement for remote patient monitoring, too. Dhruva said there is a dearth of evidence showing the value of remote monitoring generally and of smart knees in particular, though taxpayers have been subsidizing it. “In general, the field is in need of much more rigorous data.” Then there are the privacy concerns - the implications of what happens when someone the patient doesn’t want to get the data does. Overall, these devices are dealing with “quite a bit of data, and oftentimes the issue really crystallizes around patients’ not understanding the information collection, use, and disclosure,” said Kate Black, a health data privacy lawyer not involved with the Russak or Murphy cases. Consent standards for devices such as a smart knee “should be quite high,” she said, because, unlike a wearable product, an implanted device stays in for years. “Every step you take, they know every step you take,” Russak said. items.originalTitle: ‘Medicare for All’ Is Back on Drawing Board. Does It Stand a Better Chance This Time?
items.author: Julie Rovner
items.title: ‘Medicare for All’ Is Back on Drawing Board. Does It Stand a Better Chance This Time?
items.summary: History doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That’s certainly true of the coming fight over “Medicare for All.” The midterm elections saw victories by several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail. But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there have cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act — which, despite incendiary politics, made incremental reforms — barely squeaked into law after similar disputes in 2009. And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem. ‘It’s Cosplay’ So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish? For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase “Medicare for All” actually means. “It’s cosplay,” said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. “When you say ‘Medicare for All,’ people think ‘Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.’” Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF’s public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters. “I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs,” she said of survey respondents’ support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. “I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program.” What the Health? From KFF Health News A Blue Wave Hits Healthcare Episode 470 Nov. 5, 2026 The predicted blue wave in the 2026 midterms not only appeared — it overperformed, with Democrats sweeping into majorities in the House and Senate. That sets up a new focus on health policy, with Democrats seeking to undo cuts imposed by President Donald Trump and the GOP-led Congress and advance their own agenda to increase coverage and lower costs. In this special episode, host Julie Rovner is joined by Mollyann Brodie, executive vice president and chief operating officer at KFF; Larry Levitt, KFF’s executive vice president for health policy; and Amanda Seitz, Washington health policy reporter for KFF Health News. Listen Now Medicare Faces Headwinds A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program is projected to become insolvent in 2033 . Costs are rising for Medicare beneficiaries as well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates. The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump’s second term began. “Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs,” Brodie said. There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York voiced support for expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children. Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as “ a socialist takeover of our healthcare system ” — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof. Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It’s the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones. A Deeper Dissatisfaction? There is one big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. During the Clinton-era health reform debate, those people were represented in the famous “ Harry and Louise ” ads sponsored by the health insurance industry, featuring a couple at their kitchen table worrying that proposed changes would leave them worse off financially. KFF’s September tracking poll found instead that not only was the professed support for Medicare for All at its highest since the organization started regularly asking about it, but also a majority of respondents said they would support the policy even if it meant eliminating the private insurance industry. That’s a first, and a significant change at that. It suggests the public is so fed up with the status quo that they’d rather risk something completely new than stick with what they have. Of course, that sentiment could change fast when industry opposition revs up its counter-campaign. Still, the survey results suggest the next health reform debate could start with a public ready for something bigger. Now it’s up to the people who could make it happen to get on the same page. items.originalTitle: With Thanksgiving Approaching, Antipoverty Groups Call on Albany to Replace Stolen SNAP Benefits
items.author: Rosa Goldensohn
items.title: With Thanksgiving Approaching, Antipoverty Groups Call on Albany to Replace Stolen SNAP Benefits
items.summary: Last holiday season is not a happy memory for Oybek, 19, and his family in Bensonhurst. “The whole month sucked,” he said. His mother, a home care attendant, tried to pay for groceries at the supermarket — only to find that the family’s food assistance for the month had been stolen. They were among the thousands of New Yorkers who rely on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to eat and who’ve been swindled by a now-common form of fraud that targets benefit cards . That meant a food squeeze for the whole family: no more apples or bananas, a pared-down celebration for their big holiday, New Years. The soup they ate often that month required few ingredients, he noticed — half a carrot, a potato, barely any meat and a whole lot of water. “I’d just, like, open the fridge, looking for some snacks, and yeah, just go for water at the end,” he said. The CUNY student and his parents tried to keep things as normal as they could for his kid sister. “All of us had to like, keep it up, because my sister is still six, and no one wants a kid to know that their parents are financially struggling,” he said. The family thought the stolen benefits might be replaced. But Congress in 2024 stopped refunding SNAP for users who lose it to theft — and neither the city nor state have moved to fill the gap. Stolen Food Stamp Funds Leave Thousands Hungry as New York Sleeps on Reforms The Trump administration has chipped away at SNAP from all sides, restricting eligibility, tightening work requirements and shifting the funding burden further onto states in last year’s H.R.1, the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” In New York City, enrollment dropped by nearly 175,000 between July 2025 and August 2026, despite high food prices and steady reported need . A new proposed rule would kick millions more people off nationwide . In a letter to Gov. Kathy Hochul this month, more than 150 groups called on the state to create a compensation fund to repay families whose SNAP is stolen in its upcoming budget, among other interventions. The Food Bank for New York City, New York State American Academy of Pediatrics, United Way of New York City and YMCA of Greater New York were among those who joined that call, as did many city service providers who have been pressing for reimbursements in Albany — as yet, to no avail. Asked whether the state would take up such a fund and what families who lose benefits should do in the meantime, the governor’s office indicated that it would look to Washington for solutions. “EBT skimming is a national problem, and we look forward to working with the incoming Democratic majority in Congress to ensure New Yorkers get the assistance they deserve,” spokesperson Jonah Allon said in a statement. The Chinese-American Planning Council, which organized the letter along with the advocacy group Hunger Solutions New York and where Oybek is now an intern, said the state needs to step in to counter federal changes. “EBT skimming is a national problem, but with H.R.1 cutting SNAP, New York is best positioned to protect its own residents,” said Wayne Ho, the group’s president and CEO. While the governor deserved credit for moving the state to chip cards this year, Ho said, “New York should pair that prevention with a fund that makes families whole whenever their benefits are stolen.” California, under state law, does reimburse benefits lost to theft, and has already instituted credit card industry-standard chip-and-tap EBT cards that prevent fraud in the first place, along with algorithmic fraud detection. But even with those improvements, some fraud persists. Chip cards are supposed to roll out in New York some time in the first quarter of next year, the governor’s office announced this summer . Queens Assemblymember Jessica González-Rojas tried for a state-backed compensation fund in the last legislative session, but neither the Assembly nor the governor made it a priority. She plans to try again in the next session, which starts in January, when she will become a state senator. “Families in the past two years have not been made whole, and you know, that’s real loss, that’s literally food that’s not on their table,” González-Rojas said in an interview. “It’s a policy failure that we’re still dealing with this, and they should have acted much quicker.” New York City no longer collects reports of stolen SNAP benefits, but when the federal government did reimburse the claims and the city had that data, the refunds totaled on average $2.6 million a month. Earlier this year, in a survey of 827 city SNAP recipients conducted by the nonprofit Community Service Society, 31% of respondents said they had been a victim of such fraud in the past three years. The Department of Social Services received an average of 7,000 claims a month in 2024. A new report from the city’s Robin Hood foundation also recommends the fund. Asked if Robin Hood could itself step in and fill the gap, director of policy research and initiatives Chloe Sarnoff said it was a job for government. “We cannot backfill the social safety net,” she said. At a press conference earlier this month, asked whether the city would consider refunding the lost food money, Mayor Zohran Mamdani demurred. “That’s something we’re going to continue to work with the state on, to ensure that we’re protecting New Yorkers to the best of our ability,” he said. Robin Hood and Columbia University’s Center on Poverty and Social Policy found in their new report that nearly a third of city residents experienced food hardship last year, meaning they “sometimes or often ran out of food or worried it would run out before they had money to buy more.” About 15%, nearly 1.3 million people, turned to free food providers like food pantries, the report said. At a grocery store on Myrtle Avenue in Brooklyn, cashier Kim braced for one of the least festive parts of her holiday season: assisting customers who try to check out — only to find that their SNAP benefits have been pilfered. Just last month, she said, she helped a man check his $300 balance, and by the time he had finished shopping, all but $9 was gone. It seems a more frequent occurrence than ever, Kim told The City Reporter, and “it’s heartbreaking.” “And now, they don’t want to return the money,” she said. “Before, when it first started, they would return the money.” Ron Roberg, 72, of Pelham Parkway in the Bronx, was at the checkout at Key Food when he found his full $306 food benefit had been stolen. “The cashier told me, ‘Ron, you got 13 cents,’” he recalled. Roberg was already unsure about Thanksgiving plans this year. After his wife’s death a year and a half ago, holidays are in flux. But at least, if nothing else panned out, the retired electrician and lifelong New Yorker could cook himself a special dinner. And he still will, he resolves, even though he’s not sure how the rest of the month will go. “It leaves me constricted,” he said. “I was hoping that there would be some way of getting recompensated, considering it was stolen.” Our nonprofit newsroom relies on donations from readers to sustain our local reporting and keep it free for all New Yorkers. items.originalTitle: The lost education of a Maine boy held down and isolated 200 times
items.author: Lana Cohen
items.title: The lost education of a Maine boy held down and isolated 200 times
items.summary: “They weren’t really seeing me as me,” Max Dupuis said of his time in third grade in Saco. “They were just seeing me as the kid who acts out.” Photo by Kristian Moravec. Max Dupuis lay face up on the floor while two adults pinned down his arms and a third adult held down his legs. The 10-year-old boy was being restrained by the staff at the Eslie J. Parquette School in Saco, a special purpose private school for children with intellectual disabilities and behavioral challenges run by the mental health nonprofit Sweetser. On that day in 2021, Max hadn’t wanted to leave art class. His friend hadn’t either. Staff told Max and his friend they could be rewarded if they went to their academic classrooms as directed, but the two weren’t swayed. Instead, they tried to leave the school. Max climbed on the tables and “attempted to use a tool in the art room as a weapon,” according to an incident report. Staff intervened, grabbing Max by his armpits and removing him from the room. He tried to punch and kick them. They held him down for five minutes. Over the next two hours, Max exploded. He ran out of the school building. He threw things. He punched and kicked people. Staff restrained him for an additional 54 minutes. Maine’s 45 special purpose private schools, run by 23 different organizations, are presented as a solution for kids who struggle in public school. While some kids thrive in the specialized schools, others, including Max, have found they are no better off and are routinely subjected to punitive discipline known to harm children. Special purpose private schools provide a place for public schools to send students when they feel they can no longer adequately serve them. But there’s a trade-off: Public schools have to foot the bill for the private schooling, which averaged $80,000 per student in 2025, putting additional pressure on school budgets and taxpayers. In recent years, it’s a deal public school districts have made more often. Enrollment in special purpose private schools has risen dramatically over the past decade. Costs have climbed even more. The number of students attending special purpose private schools has increased by about 40 percent over 10 years, and spending has more than doubled, according to data from the Maine Department of Education. Yet their success is mixed. Max and his family said the special purpose private schools he attended caused more harm than good. Under federal law, school districts must teach students with learning disabilities and do so in the least restrictive setting possible. But determining that environment is rarely straightforward. More than a dozen lawyers, educators and advocates told The Maine Monitor that many public schools in Maine lack the capacity or expertise to manage the most challenging kids themselves. As the number of students with disabilities and instances of challenging behavior rise, they said, schools are overusing the relief valve of special purpose private schools. Today, Max is 15. He creates intricate Lego structures, goes fishing, plays video games, builds forts with his friends and spars with his parents over curfew. He attends public school and hasn’t been restrained or secluded in more than two years. But his path was traumatic and left his parents feeling abandoned by Maine’s school system. • • • One day in first grade, Max, then 7, made a paper airplane. His teacher at Saco’s Governor John Fairfield School told him it was inappropriate, and it was thrown away, according to an incident report. Max “began being disruptive,” the report stated, and the teacher called for backup. He was standing on a radiator throwing small items at his classmates when two education technicians arrived. They took him to the “quiet room,” an unfurnished 6.5-by-10-foot space, where he remained for 15 minutes. From the start, Max was a challenging kid, said his mother, Angela Dupuis of Saco. She described the work of getting Max to nap as a toddler as “three-plus-hour standoffs.” Later, when she told him “no” or gave him timeouts, he simply refused to listen. Angela and her husband, Steve Dupuis, found effective ways to work with Max. But school proved challenging. He wouldn’t put his shoes in the correct place or do classwork when asked. He didn’t behave as expected. For six years, starting in first grade, life for Max and his family unfurled into an overwhelming battle to help him as his mental health deteriorated and his behavior worsened. “I didn’t know when this would end or if it would ever end,” Angela said. During that time, Max enrolled in five schools: his district elementary schools and three special purpose private schools. He had hundreds of altercations with school staff, his parents and police. Therapists, behavioral specialists, special education specialists and psychologists evaluated him. He received diagnoses of emotional disturbance, anxiety, depression, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, oppositional defiant disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder from his experience at school. He was prescribed a dozen different medications, made multiple trips to the hospital and missed out on years of academic learning and opportunities to socialize. Angela and Steve Dupuis, pictured at left and right, found effective ways to work with Max, now 15, center. But school proved challenging. Photo by Kristian Moravec. In those six years, school staff restrained or secluded him more than 200 times, forcibly holding him down for a total of 14 hours, sometimes by as many as four adults, according to 246 pages of incident reports reviewed by The Maine Monitor . When kids are acting aggressively or running away, they’re often having automatic fight-or-flight responses they can’t control, according to psychologists and other experts. Their brain is telling them they are in danger, and they are reacting. Children in this state of extreme distress often cannot hear what others say, reason their way through a situation or ask for help. By the time children reach the point of crisis, physically restraining or isolating them might prevent others from being injured, but it compounds children’s distress and can lead to serious long-term emotional harm. Many kids who are subject to restraint and seclusion already have a history of trauma, said J. Stuart Ablon, a child and adolescent psychologist at Massachusetts General Hospital and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School. Being locked in a seclusion room or held against their will retraumatizes them, he said, causing their brains to spiral out of control and leading to long-term developmental damage. In turn, this damage makes it harder for them to develop the skills — including regulating their emotions, managing frustration and navigating social situations — to behave as expected. “It’s a vicious cycle,” Ablon said. Instead of restraining and secluding kids, educators need to proactively understand what might cause children to escalate, said Ross Greene, a clinical child psychologist in Freeport. Educators can better avoid crises if they identify, discuss, change or temporarily remove expectations that children are struggling to meet. The Saco School Department said staff use restraint and seclusion only as a last resort when students pose a danger to themselves or others, and when less restrictive interventions have failed or are inappropriate. But in 2021, in response to a complaint, the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights stated it had concerns about the Saco School Department’s restraint and seclusion of 14 students, including Max, between 2017 and 2020. The agency found that the district failed to provide students with an adequate education by repeatedly restraining, secluding and sending them home early. It also found that the district failed to assess how its treatment of children affected their education and to accurately report restraints to the government. For Max, the upheaval resulted in him spending less than half of each academic year in school from third through sixth grade. Angela, a cognitive behavioral nurse practitioner, reduced her work hours and eventually took two years off to care for him. She and Steve, a master locksmith, borrowed money from family and took out a home equity loan to cover their bills. • • • Max’s first-grade pickup took place in the cafeteria. Most days, as other students headed to their parents alone, Max’s first-grade teacher would walk him to Angela and share concerns about his behavior. As the year went on, Angela began to dread pickup. “I would try to be neutral, positive and appreciative,” she said. “I wanted to prove I was a good parent.” By January of Max’s first-grade year, when Max was 7, Angela and Steve had switched into high gear. They communicated regularly with his teacher, principal and other school employees, according to copies of their emails. They read books and talked to experts. They had Max professionally evaluated and worked with the school to create an individualized education plan to support him. With Max often out of school, Angela Dupuis, left, reduced her work hours as a nurse practitioner and later took two years off to care for him. Photo by Kristian Moravec. But from early on, Angela and Steve felt at odds with the Saco school district. They tried to collaborate, they said. They told his teachers what worked best for him at home: speaking to him like an adult, helping him assess why certain tasks were hard and altering activities so he would readily participate. But Angela and Steve got the sense that the school district believed Max, not the district’s tactics, needed to change. “There was never any self-reflection on behalf of the adults,” Steve said. Some of the district’s practices, such as helping Max name his emotions, were helpful, Angela and Steve said. But others, such as offering rewards and closely tracking his behavior with daily report cards, caused Max to temporarily repress his emotions and did not address the root causes of his behavior. Saco School Department Superintendent Jeremy Ray said the district could not speak about specific students due to federal privacy laws. Behavior is a form of communication, mental health professionals said. “It’s a child’s way of saying, ‘Something is not right in my world,’” said Carrie Woodcock, executive director of Maine Parent Federation, a disability rights group. Schools’ reward-based behavior management approaches assume students can behave as expected but lack the will to do so. But in reality, children may be acting out because they can’t cope with their anxiety and frustration. “Being able to manage and control your behavior requires a lot of different skills,” Ablon said. “Not all kids develop those skills at the same rate as their peers.” Many Maine teachers lack the training to help kids safely and calmly deal with their emotions. Fewer than a third of teachers received any behavior or classroom management training during the 2022 to 2024 school years, according to a Maine Education Policy Research Institute report. Without adequate coaching, the same report warned, educators are more likely to rely on punitive practices, including restraint and seclusion. At the same time, school staff fear for their own safety. Up to 40 percent of Maine teachers have received a minor injury, and 23 percent have experienced a major injury during behavioral crises according to the same report. In recent years, the Saco school district has standardized its practices across schools for supporting students with behavioral challenges, Ray said. The district has increased training and brought on additional behavior experts. The number of restraints and seclusions dropped from 451 in the 2017-2018 school year, when Max was in kindergarten, to 43 in the 2025-2026 school year. Max Dupuis played basketball outside his home in Saco on Nov. 1. Photo by Kristian Moravec. Max’s conduct fluctuated, but overall, it was clear to Angela and Steve that their son was increasingly struggling. In first grade, he stopped being able to sleep by himself, Angela said. In second grade, a behavioral analyst heard Max repeatedly say to himself, “I’m bad.” In third grade, Angela told Max that he had broken his behavioral specialist’s nose, prompting Max to try to break his own nose. At times, he denied himself access to music and games, telling his parents he didn’t deserve them, according to a psychological evaluation. By then, he was in a siloed special education program operating out of a basement room with cinderblock walls and quarter windows that he described as cramped, noisy and dark. “They weren’t really seeing me as me,” Max said in a recent interview. “They were just seeing me as the kid who acts out.” Max hated school. His mother hated bringing him. Each morning when Angela dropped Max off, she watched him disappear into the building with his small, red backpack slung over his shoulders, and cry. In November of Max’s third-grade year, Angela got a call to pick up Max early, by then a regular occurrence. He had run away and tried to stab staff with glass he found in the dugout of the softball field adjacent to the school. The police came. Max had climbed the mats in the seclusion room and torn casing off the pipes. He had bitten a police officer and a teacher. He wasn’t calming down. Angela arrived 10 minutes later and found Max sitting in a chair, being held down by four adults. “Everyone looked spooked,” she said. “No one looked like they had any confidence that they could get the situation under control.” The staff released Max, and Angela told everyone to leave the room. She worked to calm him down. She sat on the floor. She kept her breathing slow, her voice calm and her body relaxed, she said. Max became himself again. Steve arrived soon after. Max cleaned up the room and apologized to the staff. As the family left, Angela told Max he wouldn’t be going back. • • • Instead, Max went to the Eslie J. Parquette School, the special purpose private school in Saco. The campus is idyllic. One day in May, an alpaca grazed near the entrance. A barn housed chickens, baby lambs and a horse named Tricky. The school has success stories. When Kaidyn Blodgett first arrived there his freshman year of high school, he had little trust in the adults around him, he said. He would leave class without permission and threaten staff. But the adults — his clinicians, teachers and ed techs — stuck with him. They never restrained or secluded him. “Once I realized I was somewhere where people wanted to help me, I was doing better,” said Blodgett, who was 17 when he spoke to The Monitor . For Angela and Steve, the school offered hope. “I thought: This is finally the answer,” Steve said. “This is going to help him get back on track.” But after starting at the school in June 2021, Max’s mental health declined further. His behavior became more extreme. He dreaded going to school, he said. His heart raced as he arrived on campus. He was embarrassed that he wasn’t in programs alongside his peers. During times of crisis, often following arguments with classmates or demands he didn’t want to comply with, he pulled down ceiling tiles and removed fixtures from school bathrooms. He threatened other students and threw rocks and sticks at school employees. He ran away from the school more than a dozen times. “I thought that I wasn’t trying hard enough,” Max said. “Things were getting worse and worse. It was always one step forward, two steps back. I wondered what was wrong with me.” Adults at the special purpose private school restrained Max, often pinning him to the ground on his back, on a near-daily basis, a total of 64 times over four months. Sometimes they held him for more than an hour in a single day, according to incident reports. Max said he doesn’t remember much from his time at the school. Mostly, he recalled the feeling of adrenaline and then of having let people down. In November, five months after Max had started at the Sweetser school, Angela was sitting in her car in a parking lot in Bangor. She had just passed her nurse practitioner board exam and was elated. Then she got a call from Sweetser to say Max could no longer attend school there. The school concluded it couldn’t meet his needs. The joy Angela had felt moments before was replaced by crushing devastation, loss and fear. She cried the two-hour drive home. “It was incredibly scary because we were like, ‘If they can’t program for him, who can?’” she said. “We felt abandoned by the education system.” Max Dupuis played cribbage with his mother and father at their home in Saco on Nov. 1. Photo by Kristian Moravec. Staff at the Parquette school only restrain kids as a last resort and do not seclude them, Sweetser said in a statement. “Our ongoing commitment is to create a safe, compassionate, and therapeutic learning environment where the need for physical restraint is prevented whenever possible and ultimately eliminated,” said Brandon Somes, Sweetser’s director of quality. To that aim, the school has increased training, created a working group to identify more effective behavioral intervention strategies, and implemented annual targets for reducing restraints per client per day. The school tracks the use of restraints with performance scorecards, Somes said. “Every student deserves the opportunity to learn, heal, and succeed in an environment that prioritizes their safety, dignity, and well-being,” he said in the statement. The year that followed after leaving the Parquette school was a hard one for Max, then 10, and his family. Angela and Steve wanted in-home behavioral help for Max, which he was eligible for, but there was a long waitlist. He punched holes in the wall and beat up his mom on a near-daily basis. Multiple times a week, either Angela or Steve called the police, and Max wound up in the emergency room. He tried to choke himself, leaving bruises around his neck, and said he wanted to die. Angela brought him to the emergency room at Northern Light Mercy Hospital in Portland and refused to leave until the in-home services he was eligible for became available. They stayed for 30 days. For the next year, a behavioral health professional spent 20 hours a week with Max. He stabilized. But he wasn’t in school and had already missed more than a year of class time. Portland Kids Academy in South Portland, another special purpose private school, rescinded his acceptance five days before he was scheduled to start in November 2022, one year after leaving Sweetser. In May 2023, he was accepted to another special purpose school, Margaret Murphy Center for Children in Saco. But there were no open seats. Finally, after nearly two years without regularly attending school, a seat at Margaret Murphy opened up. Things initially went well for him, then deteriorated. Again, he was restrained. The school behavioral analyst said Max seemed “calculated,” according to a written notice. He lasted five months. Margaret Murphy is committed to preventative work to help students de-escalate and regulate, said Michelle Hathaway, senior director at the Margaret Murphy Centers for Children. Despite a marked increase in the severity of behavior, Margaret Murphy centers have reduced restraints, Hathaway said. The Saco school district, which, in accordance with state and federal law, remained responsible for providing Max with an education and finding an appropriate placement, suggested sending him to a residential program in Fairfield, an hour-and-a-half north of Saco, where he would live and pursue academics full time, according to a May 2024 notice from the district to Angela and Steve. For Max, attending school — an environment that had long been marred by repeated restraints and seclusions — was triggering, Angela and Steve said. Max’s pediatrician and psychologist advised against the proposed residential placement, Angela said. But the school system and others in his orbit didn’t know what else to do with him. “Based on my experience with navigating applications to , there are so few options available when you have a history of unsafe behaviors,” said Dr. Rebekah Bickford, a child psychologist who worked with Max and provides behavioral consultation to schools. “No other schools will accept someone that has not been able to behaviorally manage.” • • • Special purpose private schools are designed to offer a reset — a place for students to go when they’re in crisis, gain the skills they need to regulate and return to their district school. But that return isn’t guaranteed. Maine does not track how long students remain in out-of-district placements. But advocates, lawyers, educators and other experts said that, once students leave their home districts, they often remain in special purpose private schools or get placed in more restrictive environments such as residential programs or hospitals. Schools are desperate for solutions. Along with Pennsylvania and New York, Maine refers kids to special education services at the highest rate in the country, according to data from the National Center for Education Statistics . “Our public schools are tapped out,” said Eric Waddell, executive director of the Maine School Management Association. “We’re trying to catch up from years of children’s mental health needs not being treated.” Refusing to send Max to a residential facility, Angela and Steve cobbled together their own educational program for Max. They hired a tutor, and enrolled him in a coding and robotics group, art classes and basketball. He became more actively engaged in his local church. They found a small homeschooling co-op in Arundel, called School Around Us, that they hoped would meet Max’s needs. They signed him up to attend from 8:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. five days a week, starting at the beginning of seventh grade. For the first few weeks, everything went smoothly. Then Max left class without asking or notifying the teacher. On a separate occasion, he disappeared for a class period. But over his two years there, his behavior never escalated beyond that. Max said he’s not sure why, but he thinks it's because the adults at School Around Us leveled with him. They trusted him to know himself and what he needed, and they reflected on their actions while asking him to reflect on his. “They met me halfway,” he said. • • • In June, Max graduated from School Around Us, which serves students through eighth grade. In September, Max started ninth grade at Thornton Academy — a private school that provides free public education to students in the Saco school district — in the general education track. On his first day, he thought seriously about not going, worried it would be too much. But he made it, and his anxiety dissipated. “I worked really hard to get to a place to start at a regular high school. It’s nice to have a clean slate,” Max said. In September, Max Dupuis started ninth grade at Thornton Academy, part of the Saco school district. He is now a regular education student. Photo by Kristian Moravec. The transition has not been without its setbacks. Max, now 15, was suspended from school for five days after a portion of a marijuana joint was found in his backpack. But he was honest when asked about it and served his suspension. At home, his parents said he has taken the removal of a lock on his bedroom door, multiple long conversations about substance use and regular drug testing in stride. Although Max is struggling to focus in class and keep up with his workload — which, having not regularly attended traditional school since third grade, is heavier than he’s used to — he is hoping to catch up. The family is grateful for Max’s chance to start over and hopes that, by sharing their story publicly, they can help others avoid the turmoil and pain they experienced. “We’re only as good as how we treat our most vulnerable constituents,” Angela said. “If we’re treating children this way, and that is just the status quo, I can’t accept that.” Max’s progress is uncertain, and Angela and Steve remain on edge, anxious that they made the wrong call at some point. “It’s hard to have regression,” Angela said. “When things aren’t going well, the past will crash down on me.”

items.originalTitle: Backlash reignited against plans for Wilmington work-release facility
items.author: Brianna Hill
items.title: Backlash reignited against plans for Wilmington work-release facility
items.summary: Why Should Delaware Care? Competing society interests are clashing in Wilmington as the state seeks to convert the site of a former work-release facility to housing, while critics argue the facility should remain committed to helping people reenter society from prison. Eight months after Delaware prisons officials shut down the only work-release facility in New Castle County, Wilmington’s City Council and a group of residents are calling on state officials to pause their plans to demolish the property. On Thursday, the Wilmington City Council passed a resolution urging the state to stop the demolition; to disclose plans for the property’s future use; and to “provide opportunities for community input.” The vote came as a group of residents had spent the previous week criticizing state officials for what they described as a failure to seek community input on the future of the former work-release facility, called the Plummer Center. While the state has promised to turn the facility into a housing development that would include some affordable units dedicated for people returning from prison, critics say officials have not committed to a specific number. Council members and some neighbors of the facility in Wilmington’s northside also say they weren’t consulted before demolition bids opened last month. The state will close its call for those bids from contractors on Monday. Some are now calling for the existing buildings to be saved from demolition and instead turned into a community hub that would support people reentering society from prison, as well as job training, mental health, substance use treatment, and homelessness services. “The building is ready for use for the things that we need in our community right now,” said resident Tony Dunn at a town hall meeting earlier this month. The City Council resolution was sponsored by councilwoman Shané Darby, who also hosted a press conference and town hall on the matter last week. “We’re here today to say, ‘We are not interested in a plan being proposed to us in this way. We want to be involved in those decisions,’” Darby said during the council meeting on Thursday. In June, state lawmakers allocated $760,000 for the demolition of the century-old Plummer Center, through the bond bill for fiscal year 2027 . The bill also authorized the Department of Corrections to transfer the property to the Wilmington Housing Authority “for the consideration of one dollar.” The Wilmington Housing Authority has already created a proposal to turn that land into affordable housing units that would, in part, support individuals who are reentering the community from incarceration. WHA executive director Ray Fitzgerald told Spotlight Delaware that he sent his proposal to council members in August and that it was his organization’s understanding that residents wanted the facility to continue supporting people in reentry. Fitzgerald also said his goal is to offer individuals in reentry with rent-stabilized units. New Castle property records show the state still has ownership of the property. Sen. Darius Brown (D-Wilmington) Sen. Darius Brown (D-Wilmington) described the City Council’s backlash against the demolition of Plummer as “redundant,” stating that several community meetings took place before the facility’s closure. He said residents advocated for affordable housing to be built on the property during previous discussions. Gov. Matt Meyer’s office did not respond to Thursday’s request for comment in time for publication. Future plans for the Plummer Center The August presentation from the Wilmington Housing Authority about the future development of the Plummer Center, includes a 45-unit housing complex that would include 21 homeownership units. The presentation notes that the development would be done in four phases that would take a little over three years to complete. The development would include rent-stabilized units targeted “in part” toward those rentering from incarceration. Case management, supportive services, as well as counseling and mortgage assistance for those seeking homeownership would also be available. The presentation does not note exactly how many units would be set aside for reentering citizens or how many units will be rent-stabilized. Darby said she isn’t opposed to the idea of affordable housing, but would like more information about those plans. “That’s the conversation that I want to have,” Darby said. “They talk about some of the apartments are going to be for reentry. Some could be 10%, 5%, two apartments, three apartments.” Little authority Even as eight City Council members backed Darby’s resolution last week, several acknowledged that they have little authority over the property’s future, since the state owns it. “All we can do is let them know what our constituents are saying to us,” Councilwoman Latisha Bracy said. Councilman Coby Owens also called for better lines of communication between council and state officials. “When big things like this happen, there should be an integrated meeting in which all community stakeholders are brought together, he said. “Not just certain people who are handpicked to be in the meeting room.” The Plummer Center, a work-release facility for inmates in Wilmington, closed in March, and transferred residents to a Smyrna facility. | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY BRIANNA HILL Several residents also spoke in support of the resolution at the council meeting. Some recounted the support the Plummer Center once gave the community. A few called for it to reopen, and others questioned the placement of new housing on the site. Plummer shuts down Last September, the Department of Correction announced the work-release facility would shut down the following March. At the time, officials cited a drop in the number of people at the Plummer Center, along with high maintenance costs at the century-old facility. For decades, Plummer kept individuals close to family as they neared their release from prison, especially those who were transitioning out of the Howard R. Young Correctional Institute in Wilmington. The announcement was met with pushback from local politicians and residents who argued that work release inmates will lose a vital community space that helps them become part of society again by keeping them close to family, jobs, and support systems. Corrections officials estimated that the state would have to spend about $4 million over the next two years to maintain the Plummer Center and an additional $8 million for capital improvements for the building. New Castle County residents sentenced to work release are now sent to the Community Corrections Treatment Center in Smyrna. Those who need job training go first to the Sussex Community Corrections Center in Georgetown, then can transfer to Smyrna to find work closer to home, DOC spokesman Jason Miller said in a statement to Spotlight Delaware. Some residents and advocates have criticized conditions at the Smyrna center , saying harsh restrictions and inadequate resources make it harder for people to find work and stay connected with their families. items.originalTitle: A year in, permit-to-purchase law sees implementation delays, legal challenge
items.author: Maggie Reynolds
items.title: A year in, permit-to-purchase law sees implementation delays, legal challenge
items.summary: Why Should Delaware Care? Delaware is one of fifteen states with a law requiring a permit to purchase some firearms. A year since the state’s law went into effect, early data suggests the requirement is having policymakers’ intended outcome. However, continued delays with the implementation of the law’s computer system are making the permit process more difficult for gun sellers already worried about handgun sales dropping. Efforts by state officials to implement one of Delaware’s most substantial gun purchasing laws in recent years have largely been hit or miss. Data suggests the controversial law — which requires prospective purchasers to go through an eight-hour live firearm training course, get fingerprinted, and pass both local and federal background checks in order to obtain a permit to buy a handgun — has led to a reduction in sales over the past year. But a group of Second Amendment advocates continue to challenge the regulation in court, and a key computer system meant to streamline the permit review process is still not fully functional . All the while, advocates on both sides of the gun control debate continue to disagree over the law’s merits. Gun violence prevention advocates say the policy makes much needed progress toward curbing suicides and homicides. “We have turned down the faucet, so what used to be a flood of firearms in our communities has now slowed to maybe more of a trickle,” said Traci Murphy, director of the Coalition for a Safer Delaware. Gun shop owners and Second Amendment advocates, however, say the ongoing computer system delays — and the permit-to-purchase regulation as a whole — amount to the state trying to put firearm dealers out of business by decreasing handgun sales. “It’s obvious the state is doing all of this on purpose so that we do go out of business,” said Beth Parsons, owner of Shooter’s Choice in Dover. “How many people could afford to stay in business if their sales were down 80 percent?” Ongoing computer system delays Delays in implementing statewide computer systems needed to enforce the permit-to-purchase law have plagued officials since last November. Despite processing roughly 1,600 permit applications this year, the system used by firearm retailers to verify individuals’ permits is still not fully online. A spokesperson for the Delaware State Police, the department in charge of implementing the state background check system for the permits, said five gun shops have been participating since April in a pilot program to test the Firearms Transaction Approval Program (FTAP) system. Those five dealers have been using FTAP to process permits and give the state “areas for improvement” before the program is rolled out to all firearm sellers, spokesman Tyler Wright said. Last winter, the state police told Spotlight Delaware it planned to have the FTAP fully functional by March, after initially being delayed by last year’s federal government shutdown. Now, though, Wright said he does not have a set date for when the system will be operating for all firearm dealers. The timeline depends on the “completion of the coding and fixes” by state programmers, he said. Wright added that sellers not participating in the pilot program must call the state police and verify an individual’s permit before they can sell them a handgun. While some gun shop owners told Spotlight Delaware the delay in the computer system implementation has made their jobs harder, as handgun sales are already down, Wright disputed this characterization. He said the “overall implementation” of the permit-to-purchase program has been fully operational since November 2025. What do the numbers say? Data submitted to the General Assembly in mid-November by the State Bureau of Identification (SBI), a department within the state police, suggests a close to 100% acceptance rate for permit-to-purchase applicants. Of the 1,599 permit applications submitted to the SBI in 2026, 1,558 were approved — a 97.4% approval rating. Just 30 applications were denied over that time period. The SBI data also includes a breakdown by age, race and gender, revealing that 67.4% of approved permit applicants were white and 82% were male. But while the state has largely approved permits to purchase over the past year, data also suggests that firearm sales overall have dropped. Delaware does not have an official firearm registry, which makes tracking handgun purchases more difficult. However, the number of people who sought a federal firearm background check — which is necessary for buying any gun — dropped by roughly 20% since the permit-to-purchase regulation was implemented. The federal background check numbers also show a substantial increase in the number of individuals seeking to purchase a firearm in October and November of 2025, right before the permit-to-purchase regulation went into effect. Michael Siegel, a professor of public health at Tufts University, said his research in other states shows that decreases in homicides and suicides by firearm are most pronounced after 2-3 years of a permit to purchase program being in effect. This, Siegel said, is because of the common delay in implementing the program system – as Delaware has experienced – and individuals who purchased a firearm for a dangerous reason before the law went into effect potentially still having their gun for a couple years. “The whole point of the permit system is that it’s keeping guns out of the hands of people who have a criminal record or some other reason to believe they’re high risk,” he added. But the SBI permit-to-purchase data only tells one part of the story. Some industry experts said they have seen a dramatic uptick in the number of people seeking a concealed carry permit instead of permit to purchase. People who obtain a concealed carry permit do not also need to obtain a permit to purchase, but the concealed carry permit is valid for a longer period of time, and the training requirements are similar. Bill Walters, a Wilmington-area gun training course instructor, said since the permit to purchase went into effect roughly 95% of his customers have been seeking concealed carry permits as opposed to the new permit to purchase. The most recent concealed carry permit data shows 34,813 of such permits in the state as of October. There is not publicly available data, however, for past years to compare whether the number of individuals applying for concealed carry permits has increased. Firearm dealers respond Robert Miller, owner of Miller’s Gun Center in New Castle, said he has been able to weather the decrease in handgun sales better than some sellers in the state because he sells a variety of firearms not impacted by the permit requirement, like rifles and shot guns. Robert Miller, owner of Miller’s Gun Center in New Castle, said he has been able to weather the decrease in handgun sales. | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY MAGGIE REYNOLDS “It’s a bureaucratic move to try and make it more difficult for the sale of handguns in Delaware,” Miller said. “It’s been an annoyance for a lot of law-abiding citizens.” Parsons, the Dover firearm seller, said it has simply been too expensive for her customers to pay the roughly $300 for training courses to obtain a permit to purchase, so her handgun sales have gone down by 80% in the past year. Parsons said she has endured the decline in sales by “taking the retirement savings and putting it into my business,” but the delays with the FTAP system have made the permit policy more frustrating. Miller and Parsons, both whose stores are part of the state police’s FTAP pilot program, said they view the state background check and permit as unnecessary, because they are already required to complete a federal background check – known as the National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS) – in order to be federally licensed. However, Siegel, the Tufts professor, said his research indicates that state-level firearm background checks are more effective at reducing crime than the federal background checks because violent misdemeanors or domestic abuse charges sometimes are not picked up by the federal system. Ongoing legal challenge A group of Second Amendment advocates, including Wilmington-based civil rights attorney Thomas Neuberger and the Delaware State Sportsmens’ Association, first legally challenged the permit-to-purchase regulation in May 2024, on the same day then-Governor John Carney signed the bill into law. Since then, the legal challenge has gone through a number of iterations, including a state Superior Court case put on hold, and two U.S. District Court cases. Last November, the group of plaintiffs attempted to receive a temporary restraining order to halt the implementation of the law 13 days before it was scheduled to go into effect. A federal judge declined to grant the restraining order last fall, but the group has since appealed that decision to the federal Court of Appeals. The appellate court held a hearing on the plaintiffs’ motion to stop enforcement of the permitting law on Nov. 18. In that hearing, plaintiffs’ attorney Francis Pileggi said the law conflicts with the nation’s “firearm tradition,” which was established as the grounds for constitutionality of gun laws in the 2022 New York State Rifle & Pistol Association vs. Bruen Supreme Court case. Pileggi also cited the continued delays with the FTAP computer system as imposing additional unconstitutional burdens on gun sellers. Meanwhile, Austin Evers, a former Department of Justice attorney who now represents the state pro bono, disputed that the law infringes on Delawareans’ Second Amendment rights, instead arguing that the permit law has “meaningful impact on public safety and public health.” The Court of Appeals judges had not ruled on the plaintiffs’ motion for injunctive relief as of Nov. 20. Maggie Reynolds is a Report for America corps member and Spotlight Delaware reporter who covers rural communities in Delaware.
