items.originalTitle: Delaware artist transforms sneakers into beasts, bodegas and dinosaurs
items.author: Cannon Taylor
items.title: Delaware artist transforms sneakers into beasts, bodegas and dinosaurs
items.summary: The sneaker’s sole gaped open like a hungry maw. Inside were clay, razor-sharp teeth and a tongue so gargantuan it dangled out of the beast’s mouth. The Nike Air Force 1 had been painted a pink, fleshy color. It was adorned with a scattering of doll eyes, each watching its prey as it drooled a concoction of glue and UV resin. Get Involved Jerrod Weatherbe’s art exhibition, “The Deconstruction of Sneaker Culture,” is on display at Spaceboy Clothing (205 N. Market St., Wilmington, DE 19801) until Dec. 6. The sneaker dioramas on display there are for sale. Weatherbe also has a social media presence under the name JdubCustoms, including a YouTube channel where he shares his process. He also has a website where you can request custom-made sneakers. LEARN MORE The mad scientist who brought this creature to life is artist Jerrod Weatherbe of Bear, Delaware, who transforms sneakers into art pieces under the name JdubCustoms. His exhibition, “The Deconstruction of Sneaker Culture,” is on display at Spaceboy Clothing until Dec. 6. Weatherbe’s been a sneaker enthusiast since he was a kid pining after a pair from NBA star Allen Iverson’s Reebok line. Today, Weatherbe owns about 25 pairs of sneakers, many of which he bought when he worked at a consignment store in Springfield, Pa. There, he met several characters whose interest could more accurately be called an addiction. “I would just see people go crazy for it. People talk about, ‘Should I get groceries? Should I get this shoe?’” he said. Those kinds of fans inspired the aforementioned art piece, “The Sneakerhead.” Weatherbe started making custom sneakers in 2015. In anticipation of the upcoming Floyd Mayweather Jr. vs. Manny Pacquiao boxing match, he painted a pair of Air Force 1s red, white, blue and gold, inspired by Pacquiao’s Philippines-flag-patterned boots and Mayweather’s golden shorts. “The History of Sneakers” by Jerrod Weatherbe (JdubCustoms) turns a Nike Air Force 1 into a Tyrannosaurus rex skull. | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY CANNON TAYLOR “The Sneakerhead” by Jerrod Weatherbe (JdubCustoms). The sneaker was modified with clay, and the saliva is a mixture of glue and UV resin. | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY CANNON TAYLOR “The Explosion of Sneaker Culture” by Jerrod Weatherbe (JdubCustoms) deconstructs a Nike Air Force 1 to make it look like it is combusting. | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY CANNON TAYLOR Since then, Weatherbe has made custom shoes inspired by everything from the Nintendo Entertainment System to Newport menthol cigarettes. He sold them to friends and online buyers and began uploading videos of his artistic process to social media in 2020. “People were like, ‘Man, if I could get those, I would just put them on the shelves. I wouldn’t even wear them.’ So, I kind of rolled with that,” Weatherbe said. “Once I kind of let go of the fact that it had to be wearable, it really opened up the doors for what I could do to a shoe.” He began with “The Sneakerhead” in late 2024. He uses Air Force 1s as his canvas because they’re iconic enough to be recognized underneath a diorama and cheap enough to buy lots of secondhand pairs. Weatherbe continued his sneaker deconstructions with an Air Force 1 that looks as if it’s mid-combustion, bits of debris from its body flying outward as an explosion of pillow stuffing goes off in the center of the shoe. “That was after the Michael Jordan documentary ‘The Last Dance.’ Sneaker popularity just blew up,” Weatherbe said. Secondary marketplaces saw a spike in sales of Air Jordans in the weeks following the documentary’s airing, according to an article by The New York Times . The COVID lockdown, which had recently begun, doubtlessly played a role in the documentary’s popularity among sports fans. Weatherbe’s next project was a coffee-dyed sneaker carved into a Tyrannosaurus rex skull and mounted on a wooden platform. Much like the iconic dinosaur, sneaker culture is a recently discovered behemoth that shakes our world, culturally and financially, with its every step. To represent the manufacturing of sneakers, Weatherbe painted a sneaker bronze and turned it into a factory, complete with tiny workers in hi-vis vests and hard hats. Using painted sections of a sour cream container, Weatherbe made it look as if the sneaker had metal plates welded onto it. He also added decorative gears and, most impressively, a working smoke machine that pumps smoke out of a pipe attached to the shoe’s heel. “Every time that I do a custom, regardless of if it’s a deconstruction or a standard custom, I do try to implement something I’ve never done before,” he said. “The Sneaker Industry” by Jerrod Weatherbe (JdubCustoms) includes tiny figures working in a factory. There is also a smoke machine that pumps out of a pipe attached to the shoe’s heel. | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY CANNON TAYLOR Tiny figures while away inside “The Sneaker Industry” by Jerrod Weatherbe (JdubCustoms). | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY CANNON TAYLOR Weatherbe has learned skills ranging from molding clay to electric wiring for his sneaker art pieces. Even though he extensively plans out every step of his creations, there are sometimes mistakes along the way. But that’s Weatherbe’s favorite part of the process. “Probably the best part of doing the projects is running into these problems and figuring out how you’re going to solve them,” he said. Weatherbe’s jack of all trades philosophy extends beyond sneaker dioramas. He picked up oil painting last year and recently tried (and failed) to replace his car’s spark plugs on his own. Maybe soldering will be his next challenge, he added. Weatherbe picked up his crafty mindset from his grandmother, who taught him how to sew, paint and even make “robots” out of grocery bags, paper tower rolls and other garbage. Much like his grandmother, Weatherbe has countless shoe boxes full of bits and bobs he hopes to incorporate into his art pieces. “It’s just so random that it’s hard to even label,” he said. “But I try to keep it organized for my fiance’s sake, so she doesn’t lose her mind.” Weatherbe’s magnum opus is a sneaker-turned-bodega, which he said is a nod to sneaker culture’s relationships with Black American culture and urban hubs like New York City. The bodega’s interior exists between the sole and upper section of the shoe. Peering through the windows, you’ll find itty-bitty products like Red Bull and bags of chips. Everywhere, there is evidence that the diorama is a lived-in environment. “The Culture of Sneakers” by Jerrod Weatherbe (JdubCustoms) transforms a Nike Air Force 1 into an intricate, lived-in bodega. | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY CANNON TAYLOR Two cops stop a man behind the bodega in “The Culture of Sneakers” by Jerrod Weatherbe (JdubCustoms). | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY CANNON TAYLOR Tiny figures visit the bodega in “The Culture of Sneakers” by Jerrod Weatherbe (JdubCustoms). | SPOTLIGHT DELAWARE PHOTO BY CANNON TAYLOR Tiny figures are placed around the bodega, two gossiping and another being stopped by a pair of police officers. Graffiti tags are painted over the shoe’s red brick pattern. There are scuff marks on the sidewalk and grass growing from cracks in the pavement. There’s even a fire escape on the side of the shoe. “I’ve never seen a bodega that was a fresh bodega,” Weatherbe said. “There’s always been bodegas that have been around for longer than I’ve lived. So, the sidewalk is always going to look a certain way. The inside is always going to look a certain way. It has all this weathering to it.” Weatherbe takes pride in his attention to detail. “They don’t notice that (the little details are) there, but they would notice if they weren’t,” he said. “It’s kind of like the whole cameraman situation. A cameraman can do his job, and nobody cares. But as soon as they mess up, or something’s off, then they’re going to notice.” For Weatherbe, wearing sneakers has always been an avenue for self-expression. Deconstructing and repurposing them as dioramas takes that one step further. Now that Weatherbe has deconstructed sneaker culture, he wants to make a series about nostalgia. He has a sketchbook full of diorama ideas, including a Best Buy and a cozy cottage in the woods. “I don’t think there’s anything stronger than nostalgia as far as what you like and why you like it,” Weatherbe said. “If you don’t have those nostalgia goggles on, I wouldn’t even get into shoes, to be honest with you. But I happen to have them on permanently.” The post Delaware artist transforms sneakers into beasts, bodegas and dinosaurs appeared first on Spotlight Delaware .

items.originalTitle: Elon Musk spends about an hour a week on his $16 billion foundation. Most of its 2025 giving went to another Musk nonprofit
items.author: Fernanda Tronco
items.title: Elon Musk spends about an hour a week on his $16 billion foundation. Most of its 2025 giving went to another Musk nonprofit
items.summary: Elon Musk’s foundation gave away nearly $400 million in 2025, and more than three-quarters of it went to another nonprofit he founded, according to the Musk Foundation’s latest tax filing , first reported by Bloomberg. That total is down from the record $474 million the foundation gave in 2024. Over the same year, its assets grew by more than $1 billion, to about $16 billion, helped by a $64 million gift of Tesla shares. That makes it one of the world’s largest private foundations. The gap between what the foundation holds and what it gives matters because private foundations must generally pay out about 5% of their investment assets each year or face IRS excise taxes . The Musk Foundation has fallen short of that minimum before, Forbes reported after reviewing its 2024 filing . Foundations can make up a shortfall the following year, so one year’s giving doesn’t settle whether the rule was met. The foundation runs with almost no staff. Its tax return lists three directors: Musk, his family-office head Jared Birchall, and Matilda Simon. Musk, who is also listed as president, reported working for the foundation about an hour a week, Bloomberg reported. Where the money went More than $310 million went to The Foundation, a nonprofit Musk set up to run a STEM-focused primary and secondary school in Bastrop, Texas, outside Austin, with plans to eventually add a university . Another $20 million went to a donor-advised fund at Fidelity Charitable over which Musk has advisory control. Donors to these funds can take a tax deduction when they contribute and later recommend grants to charities. Once the money is in, the sponsoring organization legally controls it, while the donor keeps advisory privileges, according to the IRS . That structure has drawn scrutiny before. In 2022 , Fortune reported philanthropy experts’ concerns that Musk’s giving could lower his tax bill without quickly moving money to working charities. Other gifts went to Memphis-area organizations, where xAI, the AI company Musk founded and SpaceX acquired in February, runs the Colossus data centers it is racing to expand . Slingshot Memphis, a nonprofit that uses data, research, and evaluations to measure the effectiveness of poverty-fighting programs, received $5.9 million. Regional One Health Foundation received $9.4 million for patient care. A fortune that outpaces the giving Musk signed the Giving Pledge in 2012, committing to give away the majority of his wealth during his lifetime or in his will. Bloomberg reported that he gave roughly $1.4 billion from 2021 through 2024, even as his net worth grew by hundreds of billions of dollars. Forbes estimates Musk’s net worth at about $812 billion as of Nov. 21. The foundation’s 2025 giving equals about 0.05% of that, though most of his wealth is tied up in SpaceX and Tesla stock rather than cash. That number swings hard. Musk became the world’s first trillionaire in June after SpaceX went public, and his fortune has crossed back and forth over that line since. Musk has argued that giving well is harder than it looks. “It is very difficult to give money away for the reality of goodness,” he has said . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.author: Angus Chen
items.title: STAT+: New biotech aims to develop next generation CAR-T for multiple myeloma
items.summary: Multiple myeloma patients have been able to utilize a surge of powerful new immunotherapies in recent years, including CAR-T therapy and bispecific antibodies like Carvykti and Tecvayli from Johnson & Johnson. But myeloma, a blood cancer, can often develop resistance against these treatments, leading to relapse. A new biotech called Caronilex is developing a next generation CAR-T therapy that may help circumvent that resistance, and the therapy’s promising safety profile could make it a potential candidate for use against autoimmune diseases as well. Researchers showed the therapy, called TriPRIL, was able to reduce or eliminate signs of cancer in 12 of 15 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, many of whom had prior CAR-T therapy, in a small, early phase trial published last week in The Lancet . items.title: Video of ICE detaining father and daughter while boarding flight sparks protests in Seattle
items.summary: Footage of Saturday incident, filmed by fellow passengers, quickly went viral on social media as mayor calls tactics ‘un-American’ Protesters marched through the Seattle-Tacoma international airport on Sunday after widely shared footage captured masked immigration agents detaining a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge as they boarded their Alaska Airlines flight. Video of the incident on Saturday – filmed by fellow passengers – quickly went viral on social media, sparking condemnation from lawmakers, including Washington Democratic governor Bob Ferguson and Seattle mayor Katie Wilson.
